justice: Street space is dominated by a narrow mixed-traffic carriageway with parked vans and cars, while no clearly protected sidewalk is visible for pedestrians.
The left side frontage opens directly to driveways/garage-like shop entrances, suggesting vehicle access is prioritized over dedicated pedestrian space.
No curb ramps, tactile paving, or marked barrier-free pedestrian route can be identified, limiting accessibility for users with mobility or vision needs.
safety: There is no visible sidewalk separation, so pedestrians appear to share edge space with moving vehicles and parked vans.
Utility poles and dense overhead wires line the street, adding roadside clutter and reducing perceived safety quality.
The road is relatively narrow and lined with informal edge conditions such as blue-covered objects and parked vehicles, which can create visibility conflicts.
livability: Small ground-floor shops and residential buildings indicate some everyday local activity and neighborhood function.
Large street trees on the right provide greenery that can improve daily environmental quality for residents.
However, the street lacks public amenities such as benches, widened pedestrian areas, or visible social gathering space, limiting overall livability.
sustainability: Mature trees on the right side contribute shade, cooling, and some ecological value.
The street shows no visible bike lane, transit stop, or other dedicated low-carbon mobility infrastructure.
Large paved surfaces, parked vehicles, and an absence of visible rain gardens or permeable green infrastructure weaken environmental sustainability performance.
aesthetics: The mature trees add substantial visual softness and natural contrast to the street scene.
At the same time, tangled overhead utility lines and utility poles create strong visual clutter.
Blue tarps, blank walls, parked vans, and aging building facades reduce visual coherence and overall streetscape appeal.
comfort: The large trees on the right provide meaningful shade, improving thermal comfort on that side of the street.
Physical comfort is limited because there is no clear pedestrian sidewalk, seating, or buffer from traffic.
Psychological comfort is reduced by the narrow roadway, parked vehicles at the edge, and irregular roadside conditions such as covered materials and exposed utility infrastructure.
walkability: A continuous, clearly delineated sidewalk is not visible, making walking routes ambiguous and uncomfortable.
Frequent driveway-style openings and parked vehicles interrupt the pedestrian edge, reducing walking continuity.
No crosswalks, curb ramps, or pedestrian-priority markings are visible, which lowers route legibility and walking support.
bikeability: No dedicated bike lane or painted cycling space is visible anywhere on the street.
The narrow carriageway shared with vans, cars, and curbside parking creates potential conflict for cyclists.
There is no visible bicycle parking, lane marking, or intersection treatment that would support convenient or safe cycling.
